questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 1's planning checklist in the correct order, from the first thing you decide to the last.
items: Confirm the object, record volume, and whether the load is one-time or recurring
Check whether the object already has data the new records might collide with
Confirm every row will satisfy required fields and validation rules
Choose Import Wizard for a simpler job or Data Loader for scale, custom objects, or automation
Check System Overview for storage and API headroom
Export the org's current data so a bad load can be undone
questions.explain: Lesson 1's checklist runs object/volume, source/quality, duplicates, required fields, tool choice, limits, then backup. Object and volume comes first because it shapes every later decision; duplicates and required fields come before picking a tool; the tool choice comes before checking the org's limits; and exporting a backup is the last safeguard before touching real data.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how Data Loader's Upsert operation decides whether to insert a new record or update an existing one?
options: Upsert checks whether a record matching the configured match field already exists; if so it updates that record, otherwise it inserts a new one.
Upsert checks whether a record matching the Salesforce record Id already exists; if so it updates that record, otherwise it inserts a new one, and no other field can ever be used as the match.
Upsert always inserts a new record first, then deletes the original if a duplicate match field value is found afterward.
Upsert requires every row to already have a value in the Id column, or the row fails outright.
Upsert compares records using the org's active Duplicate Rules, and only proceeds if no duplicate rule blocks the save.
Upsert only works correctly if the CSV file contains a column named exactly ExternalId__c.
questions.explain: Upsert's match field is configurable — it can be the record Id, but its real power is matching on a custom External ID field. If a row's match-field value finds an existing record, Upsert updates it; otherwise it inserts a new one. Nothing about Duplicate Rules (a separate feature from Chapter 3) or a fixed field name is involved.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps the correct insert-or-update mechanics but adds one wrong detail: it claims Upsert can only ever match on the Salesforce record Id. Lesson 5 is explicit that Upsert's match field is configurable, and Lesson 6 shows its real value is matching on a custom External ID field instead — that flexibility is the entire reason Upsert exists separately from Update.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: when exporting Salesforce record IDs to reuse in an update or upsert CSV, export the ________-character version of the ID, not the 15-character case-sensitive version that a spreadsheet program might otherwise alter.
questions.explain: A Salesforce ID is either 15 characters (case-sensitive) or 18 characters (case-insensitive). Lesson 4 specifically warns to export the 18-character version for reuse in another file, since a spreadsheet program can silently trim or reformat a case-sensitive 15-character ID in a way that breaks matching later.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Data Loader's Insert, Update, and Upsert operations, per Lesson 5.
options: Insert never checks for an existing match — every row in the CSV becomes a new record
Update matches purely on the Salesforce record ID; a row with no Id value fails outright
Upsert can only match on the Salesforce record ID, never on a custom External ID field
By default, a blank cell in an Update or Upsert file leaves the existing field value untouched
Checking Insert null values in Settings makes Update create new records instead of updating existing ones
questions.explain: Insert always creates, with no matching logic at all. Update matches purely on record ID and fails a row with no Id. By default a blank CSV cell is skipped during Update/Upsert, leaving the existing value alone. Upsert's whole advantage is that its match field is configurable, including a custom External ID — it is not limited to the record ID. Insert null values changes what a blank cell does to existing data; it has nothing to do with whether Update creates new records (Update never does).

questions.prompt: This CSV column is mapped to the Contact's Account lookup field during an Upsert. What does Data Loader actually do with the value CUST-10234 for this row?
options: It looks up the Account whose Legacy_Customer_Number__c External ID field equals CUST-10234, and links this Contact to that Account
It inserts CUST-10234 directly as literal text into the Contact's AccountId field
It fails the row, because dot notation can only be used for picklist fields, not lookup relationships
It creates a brand-new Account named CUST-10234 and links the Contact to it
questions.explain: External ID dot notation (RelatedObject.ExternalIdField) tells Data Loader to resolve the CSV value against that related object's own External ID field behind the scenes, then link using the real relationship — no manual Salesforce ID lookup required. It never writes the raw text into the lookup field, never refuses lookup relationships, and never fabricates a new parent record just because a match wasn't found in this particular example.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it actually is, per Chapter 1.
right: Where you track an asynchronous import job's status and download its success/error files
A browser-based flow capped at 50,000 records per job, for a fixed list of supported objects
Shows current data storage and API usage before you load anything
A desktop client that can scale to 150 million records using Bulk API
questions.explain: The Data Import Wizard is the browser-based flow capped at 50,000 records with a fixed object list. Data Loader is the desktop client that scales to 150 million records via Bulk API. The Bulk Data Load Job page is where an asynchronous import's status and output files are tracked. System Overview is the Setup page showing storage and API headroom before a load, from Lesson 1's planning checklist.

questions.prompt: Before running a mass delete of 5,000 Lead records — which Lesson 10 notes also deletes the Activities tied to those Leads — you want a backup you could fully restore from if the delete goes wrong. Which Data Export choice fits, and why?
options: Include all data, so the export is a full, faithful snapshot of every object, Activities included
Deselect Include all data and export only the Leads object, since Activities aren't affected by a Lead's mass delete
Check the option to include images, documents, and attachments, since that is what actually restores deleted records
Skip the export and rely on the Recycle Bin instead, since a normal delete always lands there regardless of what you choose
questions.explain: A mass delete of Leads also removes related Activities, so a backup limited to the Leads object alone would miss them. Include all data produces a full snapshot across every object you have access to, which Lesson 7 calls the simplest choice for a true backup. Attachments/images are a separate, unrelated checkbox, and relying only on the Recycle Bin ignores that Lesson 10's 'Permanently delete' checkbox can skip it entirely.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: both a manual and a scheduled data export's files stay available for download — and by emailed link — for ________ hours after the export completes.
questions.explain: Lesson 7 and Lesson 8 both state the same 48-hour download window applies whether the export was run manually with Export Now or produced by a scheduled export — it is not a long-term archive on its own.

questions.prompt: A nightly Upsert job runs with Bulk API enabled and needs to explicitly clear a now-unused custom field to null on certain rows. What value should that CSV cell contain, and why won't simply leaving it blank work?
options: #N/A — with Bulk API on, a blank cell is ignored rather than clearing the field, so the literal value #N/A is needed to null it out
NULL — Bulk API treats the literal text NULL as a signal to clear the field, the same as in the default SOAP API
An empty cell works exactly the same under Bulk API as under the default SOAP API, clearing the field either way
0 — Bulk API treats a zero value in any field type as equivalent to clearing it to null
questions.explain: Lesson 9 is explicit that enabling Bulk API changes this specific behavior: a blank cell is simply ignored during update rather than clearing the field, so the literal value #N/A has to be used in that cell to actually set it to null. The default SOAP API behaves differently here, which is exactly why this trips people up the first time they switch on Bulk API.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Mass Delete Records and Mass Transfer Records, per Lesson 10.
options: Checking 'Permanently delete' on Mass Delete skips the Recycle Bin entirely, making the deletion immediate and unrecoverable
Leaving 'Permanently delete' unchecked sends the deleted records to the Recycle Bin like a normal delete
Mass Transfer automatically moves every related Opportunity and Case along with the Account being transferred, with no way to opt out
Both tools let you narrow to specific records with a criteria builder, then review the matches, before you actually act
Mass Transfer Records can only reassign Accounts; every other object type requires Data Loader instead
questions.explain: Permanently delete skips the Recycle Bin and is immediate and unrecoverable; leaving it unchecked behaves like a normal delete. Both tools share a narrow-then-review-then-act flow built around a criteria builder. Mass Transfer does not move related records automatically — per-relationship checkboxes decide whether open/closed opportunities and cases go along with the transfer. And Mass Transfer's object list is long (Accounts, Leads, cases, quotes, and more), not limited to Accounts.

questions.prompt: A colleague deleted an Opportunity 18 days ago using a normal (non-permanent) delete, and needs it back. Why won't the Recycle Bin help, and what's the realistic fallback?
options: Records are purged from the Recycle Bin after 15 days, so it's already gone from there; the fallback is restoring from an export or scheduled backup made before the deletion
The Recycle Bin only shows records the current user deleted themselves, so switching to Org Recycle Bin will find it
The Recycle Bin retains records for 30 days, so it should still be recoverable there — the colleague is likely searching the wrong list view
Deleted Opportunities are excluded from the Recycle Bin entirely and can never be restored through Salesforce
questions.explain: Lesson 11 states the retention window is 15 days, after which Salesforce purges records automatically. At 18 days, the record is already gone from the Recycle Bin regardless of whether My or Org view is used — the fallback is exactly what Lessons 7-8 set up as a second layer: a prior export or scheduled backup, not the Recycle Bin itself.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the three actions available to a Duplicate Rule once its matching rule finds a hit?
options: Block rejects the save outright; Allow with Alert saves the record but warns the user first; Allow with Report saves silently and logs the match to a Duplicate Record Set for later review
Block rejects the save outright; Allow with Alert saves the record but warns the user first; Allow with Report deletes the older of the two matching records automatically
Block logs the match for later review; Allow with Alert rejects the save outright; Allow with Report saves silently with no record kept of the match anywhere
All three actions always reject the save outright every single time, and they only differ from each other in the exact wording of the error message that gets shown to the end user attempting the save
Block and Allow with Alert both save the record; only Allow with Report can actually prevent a save from completing
A duplicate rule can only use one action across the whole org, applied identically to every object it protects
questions.explain: Block stops the save and shows the rule's Alert Text; Allow with Alert saves the record after warning the user about the likely duplicate; Allow with Report saves silently but logs the match into a Duplicate Record Set an admin can review later. None of the three actions deletes anything automatically — a duplicate rule only decides what the user experiences and whether a paper trail gets kept.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps the correct description of Block and Allow with Alert, but changes what Allow with Report actually does — claiming it auto-deletes the older matching record. Lesson 12 is explicit that duplicate management tools 'don't delete anything automatically'; Allow with Report only logs the match to a Duplicate Record Set for a human to review, it never removes a record on its own.

questions.prompt: A custom matching rule on Account compares Name using Exact matching only. Two records, 'Acme Corp' and 'Acme Corporation', are clearly the same company, but the rule never flags them as duplicates. What's the most direct fix, per Lesson 13?
options: Switch the Name comparison to Fuzzy matching, which tolerates abbreviations and variations like 'Corp' vs. 'Corporation'
Add a second Exact match on Industry, since combining two Exact fields with AND will catch variations that one Exact field misses
Switch Action On Create to Block, since the action taken determines whether the rule detects the match in the first place
Delete the standard Account matching rule entirely, since an Exact matching rule can never be corrected once built
questions.explain: Exact matching requires character-for-character identical values, which is exactly why 'Acme Corp' and 'Acme Corporation' slip through — they're two different strings. Lesson 13's fix for 'too strict' is switching the field to Fuzzy, or adding a fuzzy path. Adding another Exact field (Industry) only narrows an already-too-strict rule further. The duplicate rule's action (Block, Alert, Report) controls what happens after a match is found, not whether the matching rule finds one.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a validation rule checking phone format should wrap its REGEX test as AND(NOT(ISBLANK(Phone)), ________(REGEX(Phone, "..."))) — otherwise every blank phone number would also fail the format check and get blocked, turning an optional field into an accidental required one.
questions.explain: Lesson 14's phone-format example wraps the REGEX test in NOT(...) alongside the NOT(ISBLANK(Phone)) guard. Without that outer NOT, the rule would block on REGEX failing to match a blank value, which would make an optional phone field effectively required — exactly the trap the lesson warns about.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the four dimensions of data quality from Lesson 14.
options: Completeness is addressed with required fields and ISBLANK-based validation rules
Uniqueness is addressed by Matching Rules and Duplicate Rules, not by validation rules
Consistency means the same real-world value is always recorded the same way, which picklists and standardization formulas help enforce
Accuracy and Completeness are the same dimension, just described with different words
A single validation rule, written strictly enough, can guarantee all four dimensions at once
questions.explain: Completeness maps to required fields and ISBLANK checks; uniqueness maps to Matching and Duplicate Rules, not validation rules; consistency is about recording the same real value the same way, addressed with picklists and standardization. Accuracy (does the value reflect reality) and Completeness (is required information present) are explicitly separate dimensions in Lesson 14's table, and the lesson states plainly that no single feature owns data quality on its own.

questions.prompt: Match each cleanup tool from Chapter 3 to what it actually does.
right: An org-wide Setup feature that turns every address State/Country field into a controlled picklist with Salesforce-maintained values
Removes leading and trailing spaces from a text value
Forces consistent case across a text value
Replaces one specific substring within a text value with another
questions.explain: TRIM removes leading/trailing whitespace. UPPER/LOWER force consistent case. SUBSTITUTE replaces one substring with another. State and Country Picklists is the org-wide setting that fixes address field inconsistency by replacing free text with a controlled, Salesforce-maintained picklist — the strongest fix of the four, since it removes typing entirely rather than cleaning it after the fact.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of cleaning a messy export, per Lesson 16's worked example, in the correct order.
items: Read the raw export and name each problem's category — consistency, completeness, or likely duplicate
Apply spreadsheet formulas like TRIM, PROPER, and SUBSTITUTE to normalize case, spacing, and punctuation
Recognize which inconsistencies formulas can't fix, like a state abbreviation versus its full name, and flag those for a picklist or lookup table instead
Leave blank values flagged rather than inventing data to fill them
Save the cleaned file and let a duplicate rule catch any rows that are now identical
questions.explain: Lesson 16 names each problem's category first, since that determines which fix applies. Formula cleanup (TRIM/PROPER/SUBSTITUTE) comes next, but only fixes formatting and case, not content differences like 'TX' vs. 'TEXAS' — those get flagged for a picklist or lookup instead. Blanks stay flagged rather than guessed at. Only after cleaning does the file go to import, where a duplicate rule catches rows that became identical through the cleanup.

questions.prompt: During an Upsert, Legacy_Contact_ID__c doesn't appear in the matching-field dropdown at all, even though the column exists in the CSV and the field exists on the Contact object. What's the most likely cause?
options: The field isn't actually marked with the External ID attribute in its field definition, so Data Loader doesn't offer it as a match option
The CSV column header doesn't exactly match the field's label, so Data Loader can't display it in the dropdown
The field needs to be marked Unique before it can appear in the matching-field list at all
Upsert jobs can only match on fields of the Number type, never Text
questions.explain: The practice lab is explicit that the matching-field dropdown 'only lists fields actually marked as External ID on the object' — if the field doesn't appear, the field definition is the problem, not the CSV's column header. Marking a field Unique is strongly recommended for reliability (Lesson 6), but it is the External ID attribute, not Unique, that makes a field eligible to appear in that dropdown at all. Text External ID fields are explicitly shown working throughout the course, so the field type isn't the blocker here.

questions.prompt: An error file shows DUPLICATE_VALUE on a batch of rows during an Upsert matched on an External ID field. A teammate assumes this means the org's Duplicate Rules from Chapter 3 blocked the rows. Are they right?
options: No — DUPLICATE_VALUE is a field-level Unique constraint violation, a separate mechanism from Duplicate Rules, which would instead show DUPLICATE_DETECTED along with the rule's own Alert Text
Yes — DUPLICATE_VALUE is exactly how a Duplicate Rule configured with Block always reports its error
No — DUPLICATE_VALUE only ever appears when the matching-field dropdown was left empty during setup
Yes, but only if the duplicate rule's action happens to be set to Allow with Report instead of Block
questions.explain: Lesson 19 calls this out directly as the mix-up that costs people the most time: DUPLICATE_VALUE comes from a field marked Unique at the field-definition level, a hard database constraint separate from Chapter 3's Duplicate Rules. A Duplicate Rule's block would instead show as DUPLICATE_DETECTED with that rule's own Alert Text, and only when Block is the configured action.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Meridian Outdoor Supply's data migration, per the Chapter 4 case study, in the order they actually happened.
items: Export the org's current data as a safety net before any load begins
Create a Legacy_Account_ID__c External ID field and choose Upsert as the load operation
Run a 20-row test batch from each region before loading the full files
Load Accounts first and confirm the success file before loading Contacts that reference them
Fix the INVALID_CROSS_REFERENCE_KEY and DUPLICATE_VALUE errors that turned up in the error files
questions.explain: Meridian's project exported current data first as a safety net, then set up the Legacy_Account_ID__c External ID field and chose Upsert so re-running a batch would never create duplicates. A 20-row test batch ran before the full files. Accounts loaded before Contacts specifically because the first combined batch failed with broken lookups when Contacts referenced Accounts that hadn't loaded yet — sequencing parents before children, then fixing the reused-legacy-ID DUPLICATE_VALUE errors, came last.
